changes.change: The answer 'Terror' is removed from q_transition (now Election, Coup, Revolution). Narodnism is reached through the agrarian-socialist branch: q_transition=Revolution > q_authSoc=No > q_agrSoc=Yes > new question q_peasantCommune ('Should socialism be built on the peasant village commune?', Yes = Narodnism, No = Agrarian socialism). Quotation replaced by the 1878 programme of Land and Liberty: '…we must demand the transfer of all the land into the hands of the rural working class and its equal distribution.' The explanation line defines the village commune (obshchina, mir). Layout: Narodnism moves to the free cell above the new question; the stale 'q_transition:terror' icon override is removed.
changes.rationale: Narodnism, the Russian populist socialism that looked to the peasantry and the village commune, was not defined by terror. Land and Liberty kept to peasant propaganda, and systematic terror was adopted by the later offshoot Narodnaya Volya (1879). A single question about the commune separates Narodnism from other agrarian socialism and keeps the route inside the agrarian branch.
sources: Program of Land and Liberty (final revision, May 1878), English text at The Anarchist Library (https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/land-and-liberty-program-of-land-and-liberty.html)
Encyclopaedia Britannica and Cambridge reference entries on Land and Liberty and Narodnaya Volya, read for the history of the split
V. I. Lenin (1912), Marxists Internet Archive, which calls Herzen the founder of 'Narodism'
unverified: The English translation's edition (the page names a 1997 Moscow Archaeographic Center translation) was not checked against a printed edition or the Russian text
Alexander Herzen's own writing on the commune was not obtained (the Gutenberg host could not be fetched)
That an Agrarian socialism Yes/No split on the commune matches how specialists divide the two; Zapatista and other communal-land socialists would also answer Yes
The history of the split between Land and Liberty and Narodnaya Volya, including the 1879 date, comes from reference entries (Britannica, Cambridge, Spartacus Educational), not from primary sources

changes.change: The line attributed to Voltaire ('I would rather obey a fine lion…') replaced by Walter Bagehot: 'The best reason why Monarchy is a strong government is, that it is an intelligible government.' Source added.
changes.rationale: The Voltaire attribution carried no work, letter or date. Bagehot's chapter on the monarchy is a classic analysis of why a hereditary monarchy works as a form of government.
sources: Walter Bagehot, The English Constitution, chapter 'The Monarchy', section I, text at Standard Ebooks (https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/walter-bagehot/the-english-constitution/text/chapter-2)
unverified: Which edition (1867 or the 1872 second edition) the Standard Ebooks text follows
Whether a Voltaire source for the 'lion' line exists; none was located, which does not prove there is none

changes.change: The aphorism 'A man who does not think for himself does not think at all.' replaced by Oscar Wilde: 'All authority is quite degrading. It degrades those who exercise it, and degrades those over whom it is exercised.' Source added.
changes.rationale: The old line had no source attached and its provenance was not established; the replacement is a verified sentence from The Soul of Man under Socialism that speaks to the tendency's anti-authority core.
sources: Oscar Wilde, 'The Soul of Man under Socialism' (1891), Marxists Internet Archive (https://marxists.org/reference/archive/wilde-oscar/soul-man/)
unverified: Whether the removed aphorism is Wilde's, and where; it was not found in the text read
Whether Wilde is the best-fitting figure for Individualist Anarchism (a scholarly judgement; he is often cited as sympathetic to anarchism but is not a movement founder)

changes.change: The common paraphrase 'Don't ever take a fence down until you know why it was put up.' replaced by Chesterton's own wording of the passage. Source added.
changes.rationale: The card showed a condensed paraphrase as Chesterton's words. The verbatim passage is in The Thing (1929).
sources: G. K. Chesterton, The Thing (1929), 'The Drift from Domesticity', passage as given by the American Chesterton Society (https://www.chesterton.org/taking-a-fence-down/)
unverified: Page numbers and edition of The Thing were not checked
The Society's page reports that Bartlett's credits the paraphrase to a 1945 notebook of John F. Kennedy; this was not checked

The passage concerns inherited institutions and fits the 'national' conservative side of distributism better than its economics. A more on-topic Chesterton line ('Too much capitalism does not mean too many capitalists, but too few capitalists') was considered and not used: the Society cites 'How to Write a Detective Story' (The Spice of Life), while a Distributist Review article could not locate it in either of two other books often given as its source. Its source needs checking before use

changes.change: The line attributed to Disraeli ('The greatest good you can do for another…') replaced by his 'two nations' passage from Sybil (spoken by a character in the novel), quoted to '…inhabitants of different planets'. Source added.
changes.rationale: No source in Disraeli's writings or speeches was verified for the old line. The Sybil passage is the best-known statement of the social divide that 'One Nation' paternalistic conservatism responds to.
sources: Benjamin Disraeli, Sybil, or The Two Nations (1845), Book II, ch. 5, text at History Home (https://www.historyhome.co.uk/readings/sybil.htm), opened in the browser pane this round; the page itself gives 'Book II, ch. 5'
unverified: The History Home page is an excerpt; the wording was not compared with a critical edition
The passage is a character's speech and a statement of the problem, not of the paternalist remedy
Where the removed line comes from

changes.change: The remark attributed to Frederick the Great ('My people and I have come to an agreement…') replaced by an editorial description that quotes Albion Small's two phrases. Card marked as a description.
changes.rationale: No source was attached to the remark, and it does not describe cameralist doctrine. Small's history is the standard English-language study.
sources: Albion W. Small, The Cameralists: The Pioneers of German Social Polity (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1909), Preface pp. 4–5 and chapter I p. 19, McMaster PDF (https://historyofeconomicthought.mcmaster.ca/small/Cameralist.pdf)
